c.tagline: Cafe culture and Austro-Hungarian charm beneath a medieval Upper Town.

taxi.fareNote: Metered; Uber and Bolt are widely used and often cheaper than street taxis (Radio Taxi Zagreb, Eko Taxi, Cammeo).

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the trams and the areas around the main train station and Ban Jelačić Square, especially in tourist season.

hood_desc: Zagreb's cobblestoned medieval hilltop — St. Mark's Church with its tiled roof, the Stone Gate, Lotrscak Tower and the Museum of Broken Relationships, lit by gas lamps at night. Romantic and historic, though steep and hilly; best for sightseeing and old-world atmosphere.

The flat 19th-century centre and its 'Green Horseshoe' of parks and museums, running from Ban Jelacic Square down past the main train station. Elegant Austro-Hungarian streets full of cafes, shops, theatres and nightlife — the most convenient, walkable base for first-timers.

The ecclesiastical old core around the twin-spired Zagreb Cathedral and the bustling Dolac farmers' market with its red umbrellas. Historic and central, threaded by the Tkalciceva cafe-and-bar street and traditional restaurants — great for sights and food.

A leafy, residential district just west of the centre off the Ilica shopping street, known for its Sunday antiques market and neighbourhood cafes. Quieter and more local, yet an easy walk or tram ride from the main sights.

A recreational lake district southwest of the centre — 'Zagreb's sea' — with beaches, cycling and rowing by day and a strip of lakeside clubs by night. Green and relaxed, well away from the tourist core; suited to longer or active stays.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.hours: Daytime trams and buses run about 4am-midnight, after which an extensive night-tram and night-bus network runs all night.
transit.note: The funicular linking the Lower and Upper Towns is one of the world's shortest, at just 66 metres.
transit.pay: Buy tickets from the ZET app, Tisak/iNovine kiosks or ticket machines, or tap a contactless bank card on trams and buses; a 30-minute ticket is about EUR 0.53, a 60-minute ticket EUR 0.93 (EUR 1.33 from the driver) and a 24-hour day pass about EUR 2.65. Validate paper tickets on board.

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants for good service; round up taxi fares and small bills.

food.name: Zagorski strukli
food.desc: Thin stretched dough parcels filled with fresh cottage cheese and cream, then boiled or baked. Zagreb's protected regional signature, savoury or sweet.

places.name: La Struk
places.note: Courtyard restaurant devoted entirely to strukli, boiled and baked, savoury and sweet.

places.name: Vinodol
places.note: Long-established dining room doing a refined baked Zagorje strukli.

places.name: Kaptolska Klet
places.note: Beer-hall style tavern behind the cathedral with traditional strukli.

food.name: Purica s mlincima
food.desc: Roast turkey served over mlinci, torn sheets of dried flatbread soaked in the roasting juices. The definitive Zagreb Sunday lunch.

places.name: Stari Fijaker
places.note: Legendary Zagorje-style restaurant; book ahead, especially at weekends.

places.name: Kaptolska Klet
places.note: Roast turkey with homemade mlinci is one of its best-known plates.

places.name: Gostionica Purger
places.note: No-frills local gostionica, big portions and fair prices for Croatian classics.

food.name: Zagrebacki odrezak
food.desc: Veal escalope folded around ham and cheese, breaded and fried golden. Zagreb's own answer to cordon bleu, usually served with fries and tartar.

places.name: Gostionica Purger
places.note: Enormous, correctly made version at some of the best value in the centre.

places.name: Vinodol
places.note: Traditional recipes with modern presentation; reliable Zagreb schnitzel.

places.name: Stari Fijaker
places.note: Old-school dining room where the dish sits beside other Zagorje standards.

food.name: Kotlovina
food.desc: Sausages, pork chops and potatoes cooked together in a wide shallow pan over open fire until the fat glazes everything. Rustic continental Croatian.

places.name: Kaptolska Klet
places.note: Hearty grill and pan cooking in a vaulted tavern beside the cathedral.

places.name: Stari Fijaker
places.note: Traditional Zagreb-Zagorje kitchen serving the full roster of pan and grill dishes.

places.name: Gostionica Purger
places.note: Meat-heavy menu with kotlovina-style mixed plates at local prices.

food.name: Sarma and cobanac
food.desc: Soured cabbage rolls stuffed with minced pork and rice, and cobanac, a fiery paprika meat stew from Slavonia that Zagreb taverns adopted.

places.name: Gostionica Purger
places.note: Classic sarma, cobanac and pasticada on one long, cheap Croatian menu.

places.name: Stari Fijaker
places.note: Winter menu of stuffed peppers, sarma and other continental staples.

places.name: Kaptolska Klet
places.note: Big portions of stewed and stuffed dishes, popular for group meals.

food.name: Kremsnita
food.desc: Vanilla custard slice; the Zagreb version swaps the top pastry sheet for a dark chocolate glaze, an idea credited to the Vincek family.

places.name: Vincek
places.note: Family slasticarnica since 1977 and the home of Zagrebacka kremsnita; queues out the door.

places.name: Torte i To
places.note: Long-running cake shop known for kremsnita and classic Croatian tortes.

places.name: Slasticarnica Amelie
places.note: Popular central patisserie with kremsnita, madjarica and good coffee.

food.name: Continental Croatian wine
food.desc: Zagreb drinks the whites of its own hills: crisp Grasevina, aromatic Skrlet and sparkling wine from the Plesivica slopes half an hour from town.

places.name: Bornstein Wine Bar
places.note: Brick-vaulted cellar under the cathedral walls with a deep Croatian wine list.

places.name: Basement Wine Bar
places.note: Central wine bar by the funicular focused on small Croatian producers.

places.name: Vinodol
places.note: Restaurant list heavy on Plesivica and Slavonian bottles by the glass.

food.name: Rakija
food.desc: Fruit and herb brandies drunk before or after a meal: sljivovica from plums, travarica steeped with herbs, orahovac from green walnuts, medica with honey.

places.name: Rakhia Bar
places.note: Bar dedicated to rakija with dozens of regional fruit and herb infusions.

places.name: Kaptolska Klet
places.note: Tavern pouring house rakija to finish traditional Croatian meals.

places.name: Stari Fijaker
places.note: Homemade brandies served alongside its Zagorje cooking.

landmarks: St. Mark's Church
Its dazzling tiled roof bearing the coats of arms of Zagreb and Croatia makes this Gothic church the city's ultimate postcard.
Zagreb Cathedral
Twin neo-Gothic spires—the tallest structures in Croatia—rise over Kaptol from this cathedral ringed by Renaissance fortifications.
Ban Jelačić Square
The bustling heart of the city since 1641, watched over by the sabre-wielding equestrian statue of Ban Josip Jelačić.
Dolac Market
Zagreb's 'belly': red-parasoled stalls piled with produce, cheese and flowers on a terrace above the main square every morning.
Museum of Broken Relationships
A wry, moving museum of donated mementos from failed romances worldwide, housed in a Baroque Upper Town palace.
Lotrščak Tower & Funicular
Ride one of the world's shortest funiculars up to this 13th-century tower, whose cannon has fired at noon daily since 1877.
Stone Gate
A medieval gateway turned candlelit shrine, where citizens pray before a painting of the Virgin that miraculously survived the 1731 fire.
Tkalčićeva Street
A cheerful pedestrian strip of pastel 19th-century houses running below Gradec, now Zagreb's favorite café terrace and bar crawl.
Zrinjevac Park
The first jewel of the 'Green Horseshoe,' a plane-tree promenade of fountains, pavilions and festivals framed by grand Austro-Hungarian architecture.
Mirogoj Cemetery
Herman Bollé's arcaded, ivy-clad cemetery ranks among Europe's most beautiful, sheltering the tombs of Croatia's greats beneath green cupolas.

train.note: All international services use Zagreb Glavni kolodvor on the edge of the old town, ten minutes' walk from Ban Jelačić square. Croatian tickets are sold at https://www.hzpp.hr/ but the ÖBB Nightjet and EuroCity services are usually cheaper booked through https://www.oebb.at/en/, where advance sleeper fares open around six months out and sell out in summer. The through Zagreb-Belgrade train has been suspended since the pandemic and has not returned, so Serbia is a bus journey; Bosnia has no international train either. Domestically the Zagreb-Split InterCity takes around six hours through the karst and is a scenic but slow alternative to the motorway coach.

intl.to: Belgrade (Serbia), Sarajevo & Mostar (Bosnia and Herzegovina), Ljubljana (Slovenia), Vienna (Austria), Budapest (Hungary), Trieste (Italy) & Munich (Germany)
intl.op: coach operators bookable through Zagreb Bus Terminal

bus.note: Autobusni kolodvor Zagreb on Avenija Marina Držića is about 1.5 km east of the centre, reached by trams 6 and 8 or a short walk from Glavni kolodvor, and its own site (https://www.akz.hr/) sells tickets online for over 7,000 destinations up to 15 minutes before departure, with an Obeo app as an alternative. FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) covers the same international corridors, while Arriva Hrvatska (https://www.arriva.com.hr/) dominates the domestic coastal routes to Split, Zadar, Rijeka and Dubrovnik. Belgrade is about 5.5 hours and is the only practical public transport on that corridor since the train stopped; Sarajevo takes 7-8 hours. Croatia is in Schengen, so Serbian and Bosnian crossings involve a full external-border check, while Slovenia, Hungary, Italy and Austria do not.

ferry.note: Zagreb is an inland capital on the Sava roughly 150 km from the Adriatic and has no ferry services of any kind. Croatia's passenger and car ferries all sail from the coast - Jadrolinija (https://www.jadrolinija.hr/) operates the main island network and the Split-Ancona and Dubrovnik-Bari crossings to Italy - so from Zagreb you first take a train or coach to Rijeka, Zadar, Split or Dubrovnik.

half.name: Samobor
half.blurb: Small baroque town at the foot of the Samobor hills, known for its creamy layered kremšnita pastry.

half.name: Varaždin
half.blurb: Baroque town with a well-preserved old fortress and pastel 18th-century buildings along its streets.

half.name: Trakošćan Castle
half.blurb: 19th-century neo-Gothic castle set above a small lake, furnished with period rooms and an armory.

full.name: Plitvice Lakes National Park
full.blurb: Chain of terraced turquoise lakes connected by waterfalls and wooden boardwalks through forest.
